extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method; scientists interested in foundations of induction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, testing, and judging the general conceptions (classes, hypotheses) used in induction and scientific classification, emphasizing clarity, appropriateness, and methods of abstraction/comparison. Applies to constructing useful general ideas from observations and to assessing whether those conceptions can support valid inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptions assert resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘‘It is impossible to express in words any result of observation, without performing an act ... There is always something introduced which was not included in the observation itself; some conception common to the phenomenon with other phenomena to which it is compared.’’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any linguistic description of an observation necessarily assimilates the observed fact to other phenomena (asserts a resemblance); description therefore presupposes a conception that relates the observation to a class of things and supplies material for subsequent induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement/Derivation vs. Immediate Perception
rubrics_metrics.description: A reported measure (e.g. ‘‘the animal is ten feet long’’) is often a conclusion from reasoning using instruments and propositions (e.g. arithmetic), and thus is not an immediate perception though still called an observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some 'observations' are partly deductive/mathematical in origin; they supply premises for reasoning but are not themselves inductions. Distinguish between raw sense-perception and conclusions drawn from auxiliary premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation (hypothesis) is subsidiary to Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The Colligation of Facts, by means of hypotheses (Conceptions), instead of being ... Induction itself, takes its proper place among operations subsidiary to Induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forming an hypothesis that connects observed facts (e.g. proposing an ellipse to fit planetary positions) is a preliminary operation that supplies the agreement-patterns required for induction, but the act of hypothesizing and fitting is not, by itself, the full inductive inference about unobserved cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires prior comparison to ascertain agreement (Method of Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: All Induction supposes that we have previously compared the requisite number of individual instances, and ascertained in what circumstances they agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before generalizing, explicitly compare many instances to identify the circumstance(s) in which they agree; only then may one legitimately infer that unobserved instances will share that circumstance (i.e. infer a law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must be appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions, to be subservient to Induction, must be 'appropriate' — i.e. the properties comprised must be those which will help toward what we wish to understand (either those which go deepest into the nature of the things, or those most closely connected with the particular property investigated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge a conception by its relevance to the investigative goal: classing by color may be appropriate for studying coloration causes but inappropriate for studying anatomy or function. An appropriate conception captures agreements of primary importance to the problem at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions must be clear (determinate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceptions must be 'clear' — that is, we shall know exactly in what the agreement consists; the conception must be determinate, not fluctuating, and one must be able to state the properties by virtue of which the class is constituted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure precise analysis and memory of the shared properties that define a class; a clear conception requires careful observation, extensive experience, and an exact recollection of distinguishing features. It is sufficient that one knows exactly why one groups items, even if not all common properties are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rash abstractions ('notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ')
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad abstraction makes bad induction; general conceptions wrongly formed are a principal obstacle to good induction (Bacon's 'notiones temerè à rebus abstractæ').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept prematurely formed general concepts as final. Form conceptions by careful comparison and be ready to revise them; permanent acquiescence in ill-formed abstractions impedes progress and yields erroneous inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions are formed by comparison/abstraction from phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceptions we employ ... are never obtained otherwise than by way of comparison and abstraction, and, in the most important and numerous cases, are evolved by abstraction from the very phenomena which it is their office to colligate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive general ideas by directly comparing instances and abstracting the common features. Recognize that conceptions often arise from the same data they later organize, though sometimes extraneous examples supply them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a type/standard in comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: When we have to arrange and classify a great number of objects ... we fix upon one of the objects ... take this as our standard, compare it with one object after another ... The conception becomes the type of comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a representative example or standard as a comparison anchor when classifying many items. Be aware that this selected type will shape the conception you form and may need revision if it misleads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must correspond to a real distinction (real classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The class be really a class; that it correspond to a real distinction; that the things it includes really do agree with one another in certain particulars, and differ ... from all other things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate that a proposed class groups items by genuine, distinctive properties—not accidental or superficial similarities—so that genuine general truths can be predicated of the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative, corrective process of forming conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: We find the right conception by a tentative process, trying first one and then another until we hit the mark ... If we are not satisfied ... we change our path, and look out for other agreements; we recommence the comparison ... and so generate a different set of general conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an iterative approach: propose, test against data, and revise conceptions. Keep provisional conceptions provisional and avoid treating early conjectures as final laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and appropriateness depend on skillful observation and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal requisites ... of clear conceptions, are habits of attentive observation, an extensive experience, and a memory which receives and retains an exact image of what is observed ... the chance we have of hitting upon the appropriate conception ... mainly depends on the activity of the same faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in careful empirical work and comparative skill: greater observational acuity and comparative experience increase the probability of forming clear and appropriate conceptions that support reliable induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to plurality of causes (no single conception may suffice)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no agreement which runs through all the cases of spontaneous or apparently spontaneous motion and no others; they can not be brought under one law; it is a case of Plurality of Causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When phenomena are heterogeneous in causal structure, avoid forcing a single unifying conception or law; consider that multiple distinct causes or classifications may be necessary.
